newsitem.title: USA: Florida man played Bjork's music as he shot himself.
newsitem.headline: Florida man played Bjork's music as he shot himself.

text.p: An obsessed fan who mailed an acid bomb to rock star Bjork played her music and videotaped the act of shooting himself to death, police said on Wednesday.

Police also said there were apparent racial overtones to Ricardo Lopez's actions, including racist messages scrawled in paint on the walls of his apartment and a reference in a homemade videotape to a relationship between Bjork and a black man.

"In the videotapes that we reviewed, he (Lopez) not only admits an obsession (with Bjork) but refers to a relationship that she was having with a black man," said Hollywood police spokesman Todd DeAngelis. "In his words, that was unacceptable."
In London, Bjork's manager said the Icelandic singer was "very distressed" by the suicide of Lopez, who sent her an explosive device designed to spray sulphuric acid.

Hollywood police said on Wednesday they were reviewing a 22-hour video diary Lopez, 21, left when he shot himself in his tiny apartment. His body was found on Monday, several days after the suicide, police said.
One of the tapes showed Lopez, who admitted in the videos to being obsessed with Bjork, killing himself with a .38 calibre handgun while her music played in the background, police said.

Investigators were searching the tapes for any indication that Lopez had sent other explosive devices in the mail, but currently believed that Bjork Gudmunsdottir, the former lead singer for the Sugarcubes who now performs solo, was the only target.
The device he sent to Bjork, hidden in a hollowed-out book, was intercepted by police at a south London post office and detonated without incident.

DeAngelis said investigators found small quantities of sulphuric acid in Lopez' apartment as they searched after finding his body, and the videotapes made it clear that he "knew what he was doing" in constructing the explosive device which was designed to spray Bjork with acid.
Police said they learned the London address to which Lopez had sent the package from the videotapes.

"It's really tough for us to say if it would have accomplished the purpose that he intended," said DeAngelis. "But as he said on the tape, his intent was for her to open it and be sprayed with sulphuric acid."
A preliminary background check found no indications that Lopez had a criminal record or had ever been the subject of a local police investigation, he said.
Speaking outside Bjork's house in west London manager Derek Birkett said: "Although she had never met or spoken to the individual concerned, she is naturally very distressed to hear about his death.
"There was never any question the bomb would get through, the police are very good about that sort of thing, especially in England," he said.
He said the device had been sent to Bjork care of her management company. "Nothing like this has happened to her before," he said.
